item.title: How to Eat the Bitter
item.description:
Growth Mindset

How to Eat the Bitter

Pushing through life may mean eating the bitter, chi ku 吃苦.

Posted September 11, 2026

Key points
  • People who think talent is innate may have a fixed mindset.
  • People who think they can always learn and grow may have a growth mindset.
  • A difficult task can be a moment to learn, not a threat to your ego.
Source: AI Assisted Lybi Ma

When I was a kid, my parents often said chi ku 吃苦, eat bitter. Sometimes we must endure hard work and pain to build resilience and move through adversity. In my teens, whenever I complained about homework, my parents often said I had to eat bitter and push through the difficult tasks. This was their form of tough love.

I often went to my sister for clarification and support; I asked her if they really meant bittersweet. Some sweetness is nice, after all. She shook her head and said, “There’s nothing sweet here, honey, only the bitter.” For this mode of thinking, life requires many doses of bitterness. Imagine not feeling pain while grieving over a loved one’s death; you only deny what is true.

The mindset theory can help us eat the bitter.

Carol Dweck, a professor of psychology at Stanford University and the author of Mindset: How You Can Fulfill Your Potential, developed the idea of the growth and fixed mindset. People who think that talent is innate—and that they cannot change what is inherent—may have a fixed mindset. Those predisposed toward a growth mindset feel they can learn and grow by working hard, thinking strategically, being open to ideas, and collaborating with others. Every person has merits and shortcomings. People with a growth mindset aim to improve themselves and are more likely to persist in pursuit of their goals. They know that reaching what they want does take effort.

My niece was a little girl when she sat beside the master calligrapher Mohamed Zakariya in an Arlington diner. She pointed at his tattoos and asked, “Uncle, what are these?”

“I was a bad boy, very bad.” When he was young, he got into too many fistfights. He drifted and landed in Morocco, where a fire lit inside him. In the Middle East, he learned about religion, culture, and the meaning of life. He discovered that his life could have a purpose, and knowing your purpose can change everything.

An autodidact by nature, Zakariya taught himself Arabic and carved calligraphy pens to experiment with his newfound passion—all of which may seem strange because he is a very white guy.

Zakariya is now one of the world’s living masters in Arabic calligraphy. His work has been displayed in many corners of the world, and he was even commissioned to create the US postal stamp commemorating the Muslim holiday Eid. However wild and bumpy his journey to distinction was, he did it because he ate the bitter, and he had a solid growth mindset.

Many researchers beyond Dweck have explored the mindset premise. Of course, as with any theory, mixed results are part of discovery. In one study of grade-school students appearing in the Journal of Experimental Psychology, having a growth mindset did not improve outcomes across the board. This positive mindset seemed to help students who were already doing well, while mediocre students did not necessarily improve. Perhaps some students who are already ahead think they can improve even more—success builds upon success. This particular research doesn’t mean the mindset theory isn’t useful, however. As Dweck has noted in her work, we all carry a mixture of different mindsets.

We can eat the bitter and get through the hard stuff by nurturing a growth mindset.

A difficult task can be a moment to learn, not a threat to your ego.

Use and, not but. The word but may dismiss and reject possibilities. The word and can open the door.

Failure is just feedback with data.

An open mind listens to that feedback and criticism.

Don’t focus so much on the result; getting there is what counts.

item.title: The Thought That Didn't Happen
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

The Thought That Didn't Happen

Can AI shape human potential by preventing some ideas from ever forming?

Posted September 11, 2026

Key points
  • AI may improve output while reducing the independent reasoning that builds skill.
  • The key variable may be how much human thinking survives the process.
  • AI’s deepest cost may be the thought that never had a chance to form.
Source: Image by Stefan Schweihofer from Pixabay

A recent paper from the University of California got me thinking. This study looked at adults solving puzzles with and without AI help. Some could ask AI for help, with different "costs" attached to that help, while others worked without it. Then AI assistance was removed and participants were tested again. Here's the authors' takeaway:

While AI assistance can improve human task performance in the short term, it may also undermine the development of skills in the longer term...consistent with the interpretation that skill development is weaker when AI assistance substitutes for independent reasoning.

The most interesting result to me wasn't just that AI assistance could improve performance. What mattered was what happened after the assistance stopped. The study participants who spent more time thinking independently (even while AI was available) showed larger gains in underlying ability. How often they asked AI for help, by itself, was less predictive.

The Missing Thought

I think it's fair to say that we largely evaluate AI by what it produces. The answer. The email. The analysis. These are all reasonable endpoints. But they focus almost entirely on the artifact, which I suggest is a stand-in for actual cognition. There may be another question lurking underneath those artifacts.

What thought would have happened if the AI had not been there?

That question is harder because the answer is non-existent. A thought that never occurs doesn't leave a trace. There's no rough draft or crinkled paper to review. An LLM provides an answer and the cognitive space that might have been occupied by the "human struggle of work" simply disappears.

This is what interests me about this new research. The paper doesn't show that using AI makes people less intelligent. (The authors are careful about that, and these experiments involved a narrow task over a short period of time.) But it does suggest that skill development is related to how much independent reasoning "survives" while assistance is available. Two key words: independent and survival.

That is a subtle and curious difference, and perhaps a very important one.

What Remains in the Person?

For years, we have treated friction as something technology should remove. Faster, better, and fewer steps were the mantras of technology. Today, AI might be the most powerful expression of that concept, but with a critical extension: AI can remove friction from cognition itself.

But some cognitive friction may have an important function. The cognitive stutter steps of early thought can appear inefficient when the goal is finding an answer. But, they may be part of how a mind changes and grows.

In this study, the researchers call one of their measures “solo share,” basically the amount of time people continued reasoning on their own before using AI. Greater solo share was associated with greater skill development. The important variable isn't how much AI we use, but how much human thinking remains inside the process.

That might just change the conversation. The cognitive cost of AI may be difficult to see because the output can look so good. The essay, the puzzle, and the work are all finished and polished. Everything visible—the artifacts—tells us that cognition occurred. But I believe that is the wrong place to look.

The more interesting question may be what "remains in the person" after the answer is delivered. And somewhere between the prompt and the response may sit one of AI’s most consequential artifacts: the thought that didn’t happen.

item.title: What Is the Screen Replacing?
item.description:
Internet Addiction

What Is the Screen Replacing?

Here's the screen question parents should be asking.

Posted September 11, 2026

Key points
  • Putting the phone down creates opportunities for children to practice the skills that screens can’t teach.
  • The question isn’t just how much screen time your child gets, it’s what that screen time is replacing.
  • It's too easy for children to spend long periods of time without noticing how much time has actually passed.

Screens are a part of our children's everyday lives. They can be educational, entertaining, and a meaningful way to connect with others. From my perspective, my focus isn’t on how much screen time, but rather, what is that screen replacing or what are our children avoiding? So, what is being replaced when our child has a phone in his or her face?

Social connection: We all know that when our face is inside a screen, we miss conversations, body language, and the appearance of being approachable. Our kids look down at the phone when they feel awkward or uncomfortable, but then they look unapproachable and unavailable, and the cycle continues. By putting down the phone, our kids can have those awkward face to face conversations that will ultimately become less awkward. They can read body language, have difficult conversations and resolve conflict together.

Physical activity: When we’re scrolling, we’re not moving. We’re not outside playing a sport or game, riding a bike, taking a walk. We’re sitting and draining our mental and physical energy. When our kids put their phones down, they find things to do. They find people to talk to. That movement helps to regulate attention, anxiety and overall emotions.

Independent play and problem-solving: If that phone is occupying free time, that means our kids are not making decisions, creating, or pproblem-solving Instead, they are mindlessly consuming content that they may or may not find entertaining.

Emotional regulation: Have you ever noticed that our children reach for their screen whenever they are anxious, frustrated, lonely or upset and don’t want to think about it. Those screens are a convenient distraction that may calm our children down, but they don’t allow them to feel the feelings, process the feelings, problem-solve through the feelings, and ultimately let the feelings pass.

Attention: Our phones have become the biggest source of distraction when the beeps, boops and dings let us know that someone has posted or has sent a text, DM or message on some forum. Our children’s ability to start and end a task without the distraction of the sounds has become nearly impossible. Have you ever noticed when your child is looking at his or her phone screen, how many notifications pop up? Absolutely overstimulating and too much information for anyone’s brain, and especially a young developing brain.

Sleep: Because there is no end point to any social media, it is entirely too easy for our children to spend long periods of time without noticing how much time has actually passed. Using the phone to settle down to fall asleep often ends up keeping your child awake which results in a whole slew of aftermath that impacts our children the next day.

So, What Can Parents Do?

Younger Children (Elementary Age)

  • Play first outside, with toys, read, color, etc. and then screens for no more than 45 minutes to one hour. Set a parental control where the screen shuts down so that you don’t have to actively monitor or pull the screen away from your child

Middle School-Aged Child

  • Phones can be turned in until extracurricular activities and homework are done.
  • That means, sport, hobbies, in person conversation, hanging out with friends, ad dinner without a screen in hand.

High School-Aged Student

  • Again, phones away during homework and extracurricular activities to make time for face to face conversations and sharing the day’s events.
  • Invest time in volunteering, working, exercising and figuring out interests and future plans.

Remember, the goal is not to eliminate screens, but to set them aside to make sure that they aren’t taking the place of experiences that build a sense of self as a social person, a student, and a human at large.

Instead of asking only, how much screen time my child is getting? Ask what the screen is replacing and which skills you want your child to build by putting down the phone. What skills can we encourage our children to work on and practice? "What is that screen time replacing—and what skills can we intentionally give our child opportunities to practice?"

In essence, the question isn’t how much screen time is appropriate for your child, but the answer is: add more life experiences into your child’s life.

item.title: 4 Surprising Facts About Memory Loss
item.description:
Mild Cognitive Impairment

4 Surprising Facts About Memory Loss

Good years remain after a diagnosis of memory loss and possible future dementia.

Posted September 11, 2026

Enjoying a craft is lifelong.
Source: Photo by Age Cymru on Unsplash

Having lost my elderly parents and in-laws to dementia, I was surprised to learn that a very good friend of mine in her late 60s is dealing with the beginnings of memory loss, and yet she isn't discouraged. She’s smart; she's aware of the future that may await her; and she's managing to take life’s potential calamities in stride. She's not the only one.

A new book by Zaldy Tan, M.D., the Director of the Memory & Healthy Aging Program at Cedars-Sinai Medical Center, discusses precisely that type of resilience in his new book, What to Remember When You Are Forgetting: How to Live with Memory Loss, Alzheimer’s, and Other Dementias.

I also came across a few surprises in the 8th edition of The 36-Hour Day: A Family Guide to Caring for People with Alzheimer Disease, Other Dementias, and Memory Loss by Nancy L. Mace and Peter V. Rabins. You’ll appreciate these authors’ approach if you’re seeking an encyclopedic set of facts, especially if you’re okay with a bit less of the warm reassurance offered by Dr. Tan.

Here are four of the less-commonly-known facts from the above books:

  1. A decline in memory doesn’t mean you’re losing your whole mind. Other cognitive skills remain to help you navigate a thriving life. Not everyone suffers the final stages of dementia. The earliest stages can last for as many as 10 or even 15 years, offering those with mild cognitive impairment a fair chance of never progressing to the most severe forms. Meanwhile, suggests Dr. Tan, if you’re the partner or caretaker of an early-stage impaired person, don’t miss this chance to help them enjoy the experiences that might otherwise be put off too long, such as travel or learning something new.
  2. When young and healthy, the way you live may affect the timing and degree of any future mental loss. That may mean giving up the fatty meat, eating your greens, and talking to a doctor about ways to get enough good sleep without potentially harmful methods, i.e., marijuana in any form, alcohol, or sleeping pills.
  3. Don’t fret over the normal ways our thinking changes as we age. Getting lost while driving to an unfamiliar place, for example, is no big deal if you’ve always had a poor sense of direction. If you’re losing what was a great sense of direction, it may be time to investigate. Having trouble with names and faces is a common symptom, though it’s frequently a normal part of aging. So long as you can give yourself “hints” that bring back a name or word that temporarily eludes you, that’s probably normal. So if the hard-to-recall word pops up later, relax. With actual impaired cognition, time itself won’t bring back the lost word. It’s gone.
  4. If you've always gotten by with a casual approach toward keeping track of life’s details, you can learn to use calendars, day-planners, and the like. The friend I mentioned earlier enjoys shopping for eye-catching sticky notes to enhance the effectiveness of the large wall calendar on which she now depends.

item.title: Teaching 9/11 to Students Who Weren’t Born Yet
item.description:
Memory

Teaching 9/11 to Students Who Weren’t Born Yet

What a communication classroom can teach us about inherited memory.

Posted September 11, 2026

Key points
  • We inherit history through the stories, images, and memories others share with us.
  • Research shows collective memory is shaped through communication, not simply preserved.
  • Teaching 9/11 today shows how one generation passes meaning to the next.

I was five years old on September 11, 2001.

This year, the 25th anniversary of 9/11 fell on a day I was teaching my communication and composition course. Standing in front of a room of 18- and 19-year-olds, I realized we occupied very different relationships to the event.

I was alive when it happened, but I was too young to understand the enormity of what I was watching. My memories are fragments, tangled together with everything I learned later from my parents, teachers, news footage, documentaries, photographs, memorials, and the stories our culture has continued to tell about that day. At this point, I’m honestly not sure what I actually remember and what I’ve reconstructed from everything I learned later.

My students occupy an entirely different position... They didn’t exist yet.

So, on the 25th anniversary of September 11, I decided we should spend at least part of class talking about it. For my students, 9/11 has always been history. And that raised a question that felt particularly appropriate for a communication course:

How do we remember something we don't actually remember?

The memories we inherit

I wanted my students to think about how they came to know 9/11 in the first place.

So I asked them a simple question:

Where did your knowledge of 9/11 come from?

Maybe from a parent or grandparent who remembers exactly where they were. Maybe from a classroom. Maybe from photographs of the Twin Towers. Maybe from television specials shown every September. Maybe from a memorial. Maybe from social media.

For my students, nearly everything they know about September 11 has been communicated to them by someone else.

And, when I really think about it, much of what I know has been, too.

I was there in the technical sense—I existed on September 11, 2001—but I was five. I cannot cleanly separate my own memories from the stories, images, and explanations that have accumulated around them during the 25 years since. I think that makes collective memory really interesting.

Communication scholars have long recognized storytelling as one of the ways families make sense of difficult experiences together. Families create meaning through the ways they tell, interpret, and respond to stories about what happened (Koenig Kellas & Trees, 2006).

We experience history through our own lives and through the interpretations shared by the people and institutions around us. What gets communicated to us, and around us, shapes how we understand the past.

Collective memory grows through that ongoing process. Certain stories are repeated. Certain images become familiar. Certain moments are revisited again and again. Media play an important role in that process. Edy (1999), for example, examined how journalism contributes to collective memory through commemoration, historical comparison, and the ways past events are brought into present-day conversations; and this was before the advent of popular social media platforms that exist today!

A generation can be shaped by something it never experienced

My students were raised by people who lived through 9/11.

They grew up in institutions transformed by it.

They have never known an airport without the security practices that became normal in its aftermath. They inherited conversations about terrorism, war, safety, surveillance, patriotism, Islamophobia, and national identity that were already underway before they were born.

Their generation entered a story in the middle, and truthfully, so did mine.

Major collective events move across generations through stories, fears, assumptions, rituals, policies, and behaviors. They become part of the environment into which later generations are born.

And of particular interest to me as both a communication professor and researcher, communication is one of the ways in which that inheritance happens.

What does an image teach someone who wasn't there?

Because this was a communication and composition course, we also talked about visual rhetoric.

I asked students to consider the images through which they have encountered September 11. Every image has choices behind it. What does it ask us to remember? What is left outside the frame? What happens when one image becomes the image we associate with an enormous and complicated historical event?

There is evidence that these visual choices matter. Fahmy and colleagues (2006) examined people's emotional responses to, and memories of, images from 9/11. They found connections among emotion, the images people recalled, and their subsequent concern about terrorism.

The images associated with major events become part of how we understand and remember them.

For someone who was born years after 2001, those choices become especially important. Photographs, video clips, memorials, museum exhibits, textbooks, and now social media posts all contribute to a person's understanding of the event.

The same is true of the stories families tell.

A student who learned about 9/11 primarily through a parent's frightened recollection may carry a different understanding from someone whose first exposure came through a history textbook. Someone who visits the 9/11 Memorial may encounter the event differently from someone who primarily sees short clips online.

Each source offers a representation of the event, and each communicates something.

What will we pass along?

At the end of class, I asked my students to imagine another anniversary.

September 11, 2051—the 50th anniversary.

I asked them to imagine they were communication practitioners tasked with explaining September 11 to college students then—young adults even further removed from the event than they are now.

What would they want those students to understand? What would they include? What would they leave out? What language would they use? What images? What context?

Those choices matter because this is how collective memory survives.

History moves from one generation to the next through people. We select stories. We repeat certain images. We emphasize particular lessons. We decide what deserves explanation and what gets carried forward.

Twenty-five years after September 11, I stood in a classroom as a professor who was five years old when it happened, talking with students who had not yet been born. Someday, they may be the people explaining 9/11 to someone else, and that will stuck with me.

We spend a lot of time thinking about the stories we inherit. Eventually, we become the people carrying those stories forward.

item.title: Breaking the Anxiety Cycle
item.description:
Anxiety

Breaking the Anxiety Cycle

Using the mind-body connection to calm physical tension and anxious thoughts.

Posted September 11, 2026

Key points
  • Anxiety is on the rise and something we all must learn to manage.
  • Physical tension amplifies our emotional response and can be controlled.
  • Cyclic sighing is a proven strategy for better anxiety management.
Source: Migma Agency/Shutterstock

Does the tension in your body trigger anxiety, or does anxiety lead to tension? Or do your thoughts about not having control and expecting others and life to treat you well lead to your anxious mood, tension, and defensive behavior? Regardless of whether your anxiety is driven by an automatic physical response or by inflexible and unhelpful thinking patterns, there is a way to break the downward cycle of tension, anxiety, thinking, and behavior.

If you struggle with anxiety, you are certainly not alone. Almost one in five people battle anxiety right now, and one in three will struggle at some point in their lifetime. One study found that 43% of adults in the United States reported feeling more anxious in 2024 than in 2023. It is safe to say that many of us are deeply concerned about personal safety, the environment, the political landscape, the impact of technology on daily life and culture, and our health.

The downside of our anxious response to stressors is that anxiety interferes with our abilities to adapt, think, problem-solve, and behave in ways that make things worse, not better. Fortunately, there is a way to interrupt the downward cycle of anxiety.

We usually think of our physical states like heart rate, blood pressure, breathing rate, and physical tension throughout the body as under the total control of the autonomic nervous system.

While our physical state runs automatically and operates without conscious control to some degree, that is not the whole story. We can step into that automatic process and make helpful adjustments that will calm down the entire physical response to stress. When we calm our physical response to stress, we also reduce the impact our physical tension has on our emotional response of anxiety.

Better Health Through Better Breathing

Research at Stanford University compared a breathing style that mimics a deep sigh with two other breathing techniques and mindfulness meditation. The method researchers called cyclic sighing decreased anxiety over a one-month study and improved overall mood.

Cyclic sighing is relatively easy to learn but may take a few practice sessions to master. Here are the four basic steps to follow:

  1. Inhalation—You will be taking in a double breath when you inhale through your nose. First, take a deep breath using your diaphragm. As you breathe in, your diaphragm will push down so your stomach goes out. Your upper chest should move little during this first inhalation. Immediately take a second breath and focus on expanding your upper chest as you inhale.
  2. Exhalation—After inhaling, immediately open your mouth and slowly let out all of the air. To regulate the rate of air leaving your lungs, you might purse your lips and pretend you are gently blowing the flame of a candle so that it moves but does not blow out.
  3. Duration—Start your practice of cyclic sighing with a goal of five minutes per day.
  4. Setting—Look for a part of your day when you're typically not battling anxiety, so you can practice cyclic sighing in a relatively calm state. Your goal is to build a stronger mind-body connection that helps you override the automatic processes that ramp up tension and anxiety. Practicing in a relatively safe space during a quiet part of your day will help you create new neural pathways that regulate tension and emotions.

If you are looking for a way to manage stress and anxiety that does not include yet another medication, new device, another app, or financial expense, try cyclic sighing for one month. If you struggle with starting a new habit, check out this article on learning the seven steps to better habit formation.

item.title: Are You Doing the Work You Were Meant to Do?
item.description:
Career

Are You Doing the Work You Were Meant to Do?

The surprising connection between our life experiences and our work.

Posted September 11, 2026

Key points
  • Life experiences and natural strengths shape our optimal career path.
  • Finding meaning in work depends as much on who we are as the job itself.
  • Meaningful work can be created through self-awareness and intentional choices.
  • Alignment with our values and talents matters more than pay or status.
Source: Justin Luebke on StockSnap

I’ve always been intrigued by the idea that each of us may have been put on this planet for some particular purpose. Reflecting on my career journey, I see a clear throughline that convinces me I was meant to do this work.

Virtually every religious tradition has some version of the belief that human beings arrive in the world with unique gifts and a particular capacity to contribute. Even if you don't subscribe to the idea that our destinies are predetermined, it’s difficult to deny that people come into the world with remarkably different dispositions, interests, talents and ways of seeing the world.

And some people seem almost perfectly matched to the work they eventually choose.

Think about people like Steve Jobs, Dolly Parton, or Anthony Bourdain. Try to imagine any of them spending their lives doing something entirely unrelated to what ultimately made them remarkable.

It's almost impossible—not because we believe they were magically destined to become exactly who they became, but because their work seems to have given expression to something already deeply imbued in them.

Jobs uniquely integrated design into technology, making complex products intuitive. Parton transformed the hardships of her impoverished childhood and her extraordinary gift for storytelling into enduring songs. Bourdain's curiosity, irreverence, and appetite for understanding other cultures changed how we all think about food, travel, and the people who cook our meals.

We needn’t stretch to say that any of them were “born” to become who they became; but they were clearly born with qualities that, shaped by life experiences, made their pursuits unusually compatible with who they were.

Perhaps this is why we should think differently about purpose. Maybe it isn’t about discovering the one thing we were destined to do but recognizing the work that allows our natural gifts and deepest interests to come together in a way that feels uniquely ours.

Looking back on my own career, I pursued roles that let me expand my strengths while fulfilling my needs for autonomy, blank slates, broad impact, and leadership. Over time, those experiences added up to something greater than the sum of their parts—and where I ultimately landed proved to be where I’d been heading all along.

Emerging research shows that who we are influences how meaningful we find our work. A 2025 meta-analysis of 144 independent samples and 52,000 people found that meaningful work is associated with traits including conscientiousness, agreeableness, proactivity, and resilience. In other words, meaning in our work isn’t simply determined by the job itself. Who we are matters, too.

This makes intuitive sense. None of us leaves our personality, values, talents and accumulated experiences at the door when we go to work. When what we bring is well matched to what our work asks of us—and what we care deeply about—the work can become deeply meaningful.

Another study of 995 U.S. workers found that people who experienced greater meaning in their work reported greater job satisfaction and well-being. The researchers also found that people with greater "career wisdom"—the ability to make thoughtful decisions amid uncertainty and accept that there may not be a perfect job choice—were more likely to experience their work as meaningful.

This suggests that meaningful work isn't necessarily something we simply discover. It can also be something we create—or recognize—by becoming more aware of ourselves and making choices that bring us closer to the contribution that feels right for us.

While any “perfect” job is likely to prove elusive, understanding ourselves well enough can help us pursue work that makes the best use of what we have to give.

At one time or another, most of us have made career decisions by asking, “What will pay me the most?” or “What will give me the greatest status or security?” Those are legitimate considerations, but they rarely tell us whether the work itself is compatible with who we are.

A more informative question might be: What kind of work brings out the best in me? For some people, that might mean solving difficult problems, designing something beautiful, teaching, caring for others or managing challenging operations. Meaningful work is, by definition, highly personal.

But what happens when the work we’re doing doesn’t bring out the best in us? We can be perfectly competent at something that isn’t particularly well suited to us. We can perform well, earn a good living and receive plenty of recognition while still experiencing diminished well-being because our work isn't making the best use of who we are.

I’ve found it helpful to look backward—to think about the work you’ve done and identify which experiences brought out something that felt natural and personally aligned. What were you doing when you felt most energized and in flow? What tasks made your heart sing?

It’s easy to focus on what we didn’t like, and that’s informative. But what we need to take from our career experience is clarity around what we’re naturally good at, what interests us, what we value, and where we can make the biggest difference.

I had a very difficult upbringing. My mother died suddenly when I was nine, my father psychologically and emotionally abused me until my high school graduation—and then emancipated me without any notice or financial support. I managed to right my ship, graduate from college, and go on to have a very successful senior leadership career. But it was only 25 years later, when I was writing my first book, Lead From The Heart, that I fully realized all those experiences gave me the knowledge and wisdom to challenge traditional leadership practices. I could not be who I am today or do the work I do today without having had this journey.

I don’t believe we should romanticize suffering or assert that painful experiences happen to us for a reason. My mother’s death and my father’s treatment of me were not gifts, even if they proved to alter my life’s trajectory in a positive way. I’ve come to understand that none of us gets to choose all the experiences that shape us. But what we can do is choose what we do with them.

The same is also true of our careers. When choosing jobs, we don't always know where they will lead or how a particular experience will matter down the road. A role that seems like a detour may teach us something we desperately need to know later. A strength we barely notice in ourselves may turn out to be the very thing that allows us to make an important contribution. Even the work we ultimately leave behind can teach us something about the work that’s right for us.

This is why it’s worth looking at our careers not simply as a series of jobs and accomplishments, but as a collection of clues.

When have you felt most like yourself at work? What kinds of challenges have consistently drawn you in rather than worn you down? What do people seem to turn to you for, even when you’re not trying to be good at it? And where do our abilities, interests, values, and experiences converge?

We may not have been born knowing exactly what we were meant to do in our one life on Earth. But perhaps we were born with some of the ingredients—and our lives gradually give us the rest.

item.title: Dissociation Through a Trauma Lens
item.description:
Trauma

Dissociation Through a Trauma Lens

How trauma can shape dissociation, and why understanding it matters for healing.

Posted September 11, 2026

Key points
  • Dissociation is common across psychiatric conditions and can be a response to trauma.
  • Severe dissociation is often misunderstood, misdiagnosed, or mistaken for other conditions.
  • Trauma-informed treatment can help people manage dissociation and rebuild a sense of connection.
  • Healing requires addressing the roots of trauma—not pathologizing dissociative symptoms.

By Suliana Beraki and Robert T. Muller, Ph.D.

Dissociation and its associated disorders: derealization, depersonalization, and dissociative identity disorder exist alongside a spectrum of both psychiatric disorders and mundane experiences. It is a transdiagnostic phenomenon, with studies suggesting that 2 to 10 percent of people will experience dissociative symptoms at some point.

For those with posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD), the numbers are even higher, with 38 to 48 percent meeting the criteria for the dissociative subtype (PTSD-DS), displaying a significant overlap between trauma-related disorders and dissociative symptoms. In many cases, dissociation is a consequence of trauma.

However, doubts surrounding the authenticity and validity of more severe cases of dissociative experiences continue to influence both clinical and public perceptions.

Source: Baikang Yuan / Unsplash

Dissociative disorders, particularly those involving memory disruptions, are often misunderstood or misattributed to other psychiatric conditions such as psychosis or borderline personality disorder. Fabrication or exaggeration is a persistent misconception about dissociative experiences. This misconception contributes to the isolation that individuals who report these experiences have.

Clinical psychologist and leading dissociation researcher, Martin Dorahy of the University of Canterbury, New Zealand, examines common misconceptions surrounding dissociation: “People experiencing dissociation tend to hide their symptoms; they do not volunteer them as perhaps someone with depression might volunteer that they are in a low mood.” As a result, individuals with dissociative disorders often face delayed, missed, or inappropriate diagnoses.

Dissociative experience has an empirically supported relationship to trauma and leaves individuals with a sense of disconnection or separation. Psychologist Bethany Brand, professor at Towson University and leading researcher in dissociative disorders and trauma, developed an evidence-based program supporting individuals struggling with dissociation and complex trauma. Informed by both clinical research, therapeutic knowledge, and extensive feedback from people living with complex trauma and dissociation, the program offers practical tools for grounding, emotion regulation, and self-compassion.

“Trauma survivors start to shift into dissociative states much more quickly,” Brand explains. “It helps them not feel the full emotional or physical pain of trauma. But over time, this automatic response may impair functioning and awareness, leaving individuals vulnerable to re-victimization and emotional disconnection.”

Source: Priscilla Du Preez / Unsplash

When faced with unbearable stress or trauma, the mind sometimes develops a mechanism to deal with overwhelming threats by detaching, especially when escape is impossible. But when focusing only on symptoms of dissociation without understanding why they happen, we miss the possibility of meaningful intervention. Trauma isn’t just a footnote in dissociation; it’s often the root cause. Recognizing the link between trauma and severe dissociation is essential—not only for developing effective treatment plans but also for addressing the underlying causes, rather than pathologizing its manifestations.

Healing must not only recognize dissociation as a psychological protective response to overwhelming harm, but also actively work to restore the broken threads of connection that trauma severs.

Suliana Beraki is a research student at York University.

item.title: The Portrayal of Trauma in "Furious"
item.description:
Trauma

The Portrayal of Trauma in "Furious"

Why Emmy Rossum deserves an Emmy.

Posted September 11, 2026

Key points
  • "Furious" captures sexual trauma's psychological aftermath with an honesty that feels both daunting and real.
  • "Furious" shows how someone can live a robust life while carrying trauma.
  • Before asking what is wrong with someone, let's work to understand what happened to them.

Hulu’s new drama Furious bursts with details, violence, quirkiness, and surprise. The show is willing to dive deeply into the world of sex trafficking and the violent, pathological underbelly of a twisted universe, hiding in plain sight. The themes are familiar, but the nuance and details of this series feel unusual.

And I will admit, I am a little embarrassed by how captivated I became, streaming the show much more quickly than my usual pacing. Why? I wondered.

I think it has something to do with being a therapist and therefore being invited into the private corners of people’s lives—and witnessing just how daunting it is to metabolize violent sexual trauma. All trauma is difficult to metabolize, of course, but sexual abuse is as old as time, happening all around us and habitually ignored. Furious captures its psychological aftermath with an honesty that feels both daunting and real.

Early in his career, Sigmund Freud spent considerable time treating patients diagnosed with what was then called “hysteria.” Rather than simply dismissing their symptoms, he listened closely to their stories. In 1896, Freud presented a paper called “The Aetiology of Hysteria,” arguing that traumatic sexual experiences in childhood were at the root of the psychological symptoms he was encountering in many of his patients.

The idea was bold and unsettling and was met with considerable skepticism from his medical colleagues. Freud ultimately retreated from what became known as his “seduction theory,” and his reasons for doing so remain a subject of debate. But more than a century later, there is something startlingly contemporary about this chapter of Freud’s history: the profound difficulty we can have believing, looking directly at, and honestly facing accounts of sexual trauma.

In Furious, creator Elizabeth Meriwether and actor and executive producer Emmy Rossum enter similarly uncomfortable territory. They challenge our assumptions about emotional unwellness by asking us not simply to look at troubling behavior, but to consider what might lie underneath it.

By the first episode, it is clear that Furious is not really a whodunit crime drama. It is a rich, deep, complicated exploration of the residual impact of post-traumatic stress and the unpredictable shapes and forms it can take.

This becomes most profound in the quiet corners of the lives of its two female leads—the detective (Alice) and the fugitive (Catherine). The series gives us two women whose lives have been shaped by trauma without reducing either woman to her trauma. Their histories emerge in fragments, in behavior, in relationships, and sometimes in what they cannot fully remember or say.

And this is where Rossum’s performance becomes extraordinary.

Some of the most affecting moments happen when Alice is completely alone. We watch her shake. We watch her hold herself, as though her body is struggling and starving for a basic level of human containment that others seem to possess so naturally. There is no speech that explains what she is feeling and no tidy revelation that tells the viewer how to understand her. Rossum simply allows us to witness what trauma can look like when nobody else is watching. (Several moments when Catherine is alone are equally moving. Especially the one with the retainer and the backpack, giving viewers an unforgettable window into the character's longing and childhood loss.)

As a therapist, I found these scenes particularly moving. Trauma is not only something we remember or something we talk about. It can live in the body, surfacing in moments that seem disconnected from the original experience and sometimes beyond the reach of language.

And then there is the scene with Alice’s half-sister after Alice leaves the hospital. Her sister offers her pears, and Alice finally explains why she does not want them. It is such a small, domestic exchange—and precisely because of that, it captures something enormous. It’s easy to understand Alice’s unlikability. The past attaches itself to an ordinary domestic object. A pear is no longer simply a pear.

Rossum does not overplay the moment. Alice does not suddenly become a different person because she has disclosed something painful. Instead, we watch one human being allow another human being slightly closer to an experience she has largely carried alone.

This is part of what Furious understands and conveys so well about trauma. Its aftermath does not necessarily announce itself. We often encounter it indirectly: in the relationship that cannot quite feel safe, the reaction that seems disproportionate, the person who appears difficult, unreachable, or off, or even in the refusal of something as ordinary as a piece of fruit. Behavior that makes little sense in isolation becomes profoundly understandable once we know more of the story.

It is interesting trying to imagine Freud interviewing and struggling to understand someone like Catherine or even Alice — more than a century ago. And part of what Furious gets so right is relational; before asking what is wrong with someone, we might need to understand what happened to them and what they have had to do in order to survive it.

And this is why Emmy Rossum deserves an Emmy. Her performance does not simply show us a traumatized woman. She gives us something much more complicated and real: a woman living a robust life while carrying trauma within it. Alice can be capable and careless, connected and isolated, powerful and profoundly weak. None of these qualities cancels out the others.

Rossum lets us see them all.

Viewer discretion is advised, and the show posts important information to support viewers who may find the show profoundly meaningful and also triggering.

item.title: After Facing Death, Is There Any Hope for Sex?
item.description:
Sex

After Facing Death, Is There Any Hope for Sex?

Losing loved ones is part of aging, but it doesn't have to mean the end of one's sex life.

Posted September 11, 2026

Death.

It's not a sexy topic.

But while your eventual demise may not be at the top of the list of what you think about when you consider doing the deed, death is a highly common phenomenon, and the risk of mortality increases as you age. However, discussions of sex and death are low. The fact that it, and related terms such as loss, grief, and bereavement, are not so easy on the eyes or mind may be one reason why academic research on sex and death is lacking. One way to make this more digestible and less spooky is to talk about it.

As discussed in my previous post, the happenings of life can make it more challenging to desire or want to have sex as an older adult. As we age, we see loss in various areas of our lives, such as moving on from college friends, switching jobs, transitioning into assisted living, and the untimely and often inevitable death of our loved ones. As a waiter in my early teens at an assisted living facility, I remember seeing George and Ruthanne happily holding hands at dinner. Then, the next week, Ruthanne was dining alone. I remember thinking how hard, in general, it must be for your partner of many years to no longer be there. Today, as a sexual health and aging researcher, it has me questioning how as loss such as the one Ruthanne experienced influences the sex lives of older adults.

How do we approach sex when the intense and common events of death and loss can cause such grief and bereavement? The answer, speaking from my own personal experiences and after reading a recent article in this area, seems to be a mixed bag. Research shows that grief (or responses to losing something) can make it harder to get back into the swing of things with sex. But it seems that sex in these instances can be helpful (Jones et al., 2024), which makes it even more critical for those who want to continue to have sex to be able to process the barriers that death can bring to our sexuality.

For clinicians working with clients who need a little extra help with this, Jones et al. (2024) suggest that normalizing these discussions and remaining open can be powerful for their clients. I personally agree with their research findings that the more willing clinicians are to discuss the intersection of these two tough areas, the better clients could feel seen, leading to improvement in their sex lives.

I think we can also apply this message of being more open about this subject to larger society and those navigating this issue without the help of therapy. Instead of keeping these hardships to yourself, talk to your partner, health providers, family, and friends whom you can lean on during tough times. It is easier said than done. But by talking about it, we can make it feel less scary.

The intersection of death and sex is complex and can be hard to navigate; however, just because the Grim Reaper comes knocking doesn't mean that the boat can't still be rocking.

item.title: Confidence Versus Competence: A Bad Trade-off
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Confidence Versus Competence: A Bad Trade-off

AI makes us surer that we are right when we are wrong.

Posted September 11, 2026

Key points
  • AI can increase speed and productivity, but it may also erode human judgment.
  • Dependence on AI can increase people's willingness to accept wrong answers without hesitation.
  • It's important to continue to think critically when using AI and to maintain ownership over the final product.
Preserving agency begins with knowing the difference between confidence, comprehension, and competence.
Source: AI-Generated / ChatGPT 2026

For centuries, a tiny phrase has protected human judgment from mistakes: I don’t know. Ich weiss nicht. No sé. These words created a magical pause between impression and conclusion, a space in which evidence could be checked, assumptions questioned, and conclusions revised.

“I don’t know” reflects the ability to recognize the limits of one’s knowledge and resist pretending otherwise. In that sense, accepting uncertainty is part of agency. It keeps the mind open long enough for mature judgment to occur. That takes courage.

Artificial intelligence is compressing that space. Across five experiments involving more than 3,000 participants, researchers asked individuals challenging topical questions while allowing them to reply, “I don’t know.” Participants were then given deliberately incorrect AI advice.

Without AI support, participants were relatively willing to withhold judgment when uncertain. Once AI advice was introduced, that restraint almost disappeared. Their accuracy also fell sharply, even as their confidence more than doubled. In other words, AI made participants considerably more certain while making them less likely to be right. They went the convenient path of accepting wrong answers unquestioned, while concomitantly losing the ability to recognize when an answer was wrong.

The poisoned chalice of fluency

Generative AI is unusually capable of producing this effect because it has mastered outward signals humans associate with knowing. Answers arrive instantly, arguments are structured, and explanations sound composed. We readily associate such verbal fluency with understanding, mistaking confidence for competence and specificity for credibility. AI influences more than the information before us; it can alter how that information feels.

A 2026 study found that people perceived AI agents as more confident than human agents even when their underlying behavior was equivalent, creating an “illusion of greater confidence.” We often use another person’s assurance as a cue when deciding how much weight to give their judgment. With AI, a similar mechanism may be operating at scale. We borrow the answer and, almost unnoticed, the assurance attached to it.

But providing an answer is not the same as understanding. AI is making the first almost frictionless, while the second requires effort. Before generative AI, uncertainty often forced that effort upon us. We searched, compared, returned to sources, and sometimes abandoned a conclusion because the evidence did not justify it. That friction has intellectual value because it forces us to distinguish what we know from what we merely suspect.

Today, a plausible response can appear before uncertainty has had time to register. Are we under these circumstances still willing to think ourselves—to examine the evidence, look for omissions, consider alternatives, and calibrate how certain we should actually be? These are acts of metacognition: the capacity to examine our own thinking rather than simply accept its conclusions. When this layer weakens, we lose the ability to recognize the distance between competence and confidence.

When performance and judgment part company

A 2025 study of knowledge workers found that greater confidence in generative AI was associated with less critical-thinking effort. Participants devoted less effort to generating and evaluating information themselves and more to integrating and supervising machine-produced content. Delegation is useful, but its value depends on the quality of the process and the final ability of judgment that remains active afterward.

Another recent study found that participants using AI performed better on reasoning tasks (while the AI was present) yet became less accurate in assessing their own performance. Its title captured the predicament neatly: AI makes you smarter but none the wiser. Performance and self-knowledge can move in different directions. AI may help us produce stronger outputs while weakening our ability to judge their limits, and our own.

This is where the confidence gap becomes an agency problem. Agency depends on the capacity to form a judgment worth acting upon: to distinguish evidence from assumption, confidence from competence, and plausibility from truth. Repeated cognitive outsourcing gradually erodes that capacity. The progression may start with experimentation, when AI is used occasionally. It moves into integration as the technology becomes embedded in everyday routines, then into reliance, when thinking or working without AI begins to feel unusually difficult. At the far end lies dependence, when the ability or willingness to operate independently becomes seriously diminished.

Agency decay is difficult to notice and accept, because AI may remain useful throughout. It may surface in the questions that disappear from our internal dialogue. “What do I think?” gives way to “What does AI say?” and may eventually become “Why should I think if it’s already answered?” The double faculty at stake is cognitive autonomy, which conditions epistemic independence: our capacity to determine what deserves to be believed and why.

Relearning to pause

Preserving that capacity requires deliberate choices in how AI is designed, taught, and used. AI systems should be configured to communicate uncertainty clearly. Education should reward a well-founded “I don’t know” as evidence of judgment. Workplaces should treat verification and source scrutiny as worthy knowledge work. At the individual level, one habit matters now immensely: interrupting a fluent AI response long enough to ask, “How do I know?”

The experiments offer an encouraging clue. When accuracy was rewarded, and mistakes carried a cost, participants became more cautious, followed bad AI advice less readily, and performed better. Judgment can be exercised, and what we exercise we are more likely to preserve. In a world where machines can nearly always produce an answer, one of the most valuable forms of natural intelligence may be knowing when an answer is insufficient.

item.title: What Is ‘Dial-Toning’ in Dating
item.description:
Mating

What Is ‘Dial-Toning’ in Dating

Dial-toning can be quite common after getting someone's contact info.

Posted September 11, 2026

Key points
  • "Dial-toning" is when people give you their contact info but ignore you when you actually reach out to them.
  • It's quite common in the dating world as 46 percent of survey respondents admitted to dial-toning others.
  • Dial-toning may be a way to avoid directly rejecting someone or used by those just looking for validation.
  • Direct, face-to-face rejection rather than dial-toning can save everyone time, effort, and guess work.
Source: PattyPhoto/Shutterstock

You may not like the tone of this dating behavior. It’s being called “dial-toning,” and it’s when people give you their contact info only to then ignore you or, in some way, avoid you when you actually reach out to them.

What Is Dial-Toning?

This behavior could range from radio silence—or maybe the more up-to-date term is blue-tick silence—to very vague responses when you follow up with a text or a call. The contact info that you were given could have been their real contact info or perhaps a fake one, such as the number for the local pest control service. Either way, it soon becomes quite clear that they have no real interest in pursuing anything further. This can be quite disappointing, since you might have thought that they offered their contact info so that you could, you know, contact them.

It’s not quite ghosting because you haven’t even been given the chance to be ghosted. Ghosting requires some kind of connection to have been established already. It’s also not when people give you their contact info and then later change their minds or get too busy to respond to you. With dial toning, their interest in connecting with you was never, ever more than zero.

The nickname “dial toning” comes from how most phones and calling used to work. You’d have to listen for a humming dial tone before entering a phone number to call. This dial tone would also play once someone hung up on you. So a dial tone essentially allows you to call but doesn’t guarantee anyone will answer on the other side.

Dial-Toning Is Common in Dating

Anyone who thinks that dial-toning doesn’t happen in the dating world may be a little tone deaf, so to speak. In fact, dial-toning may ring quite a familiar tone for many. In a Hint App survey of 5,847 adults across the United States, United Kingdom, Canada, the European Union, Latin America, and Australia who have dated over the past 12 months, 46 percent of respondents admitted to having given someone their contact details despite already knowing they were unlikely to pursue the potential connection. You could also say that many were quite dialed in to do this, as 63 percent of survey respondents who were dial toners had acknowledged doing so deliberately.

Why Do People Dial-Tone?

So, why would people even bother offering you their contact info when they have absolutely no interest in connecting in any way? Well, among the survey respondents who had done the dial-toning thing, 57 percent indicated that rejecting someone from afar is easier than rejecting someone face-to-face. In other words, this can be a way of damping down their rejection of you—saving it until the two of you are far apart.

This could mean that the person dial-toning you is simply conflict-avoidant or even people-pleasing. Alternatively, that person could have had bad past experiences when rejecting people. It might have been encountering someone with The Lord of the Rings’ Gollum-like persistence, such as someone insisting, "I'm not going to leave until I get your number,” or “I won’t take 'no' for an answer.”

Or maybe it was someone demonstrating The Vampire Diaries’ Damon Salvatore-like anger when getting rejected in person. The survey did reveal that 41 percent of those using dial-toning did so because they worried that direct rejection could result in the situation becoming uncomfortable or confrontational.

Then there are people who give out their numbers simply for the ego boost and the “I’ve-still-got-it” validation. They may like the fact that you are asking them for their contact info but not like you per se. For example, a couple I knew used to go to parties and then compete with each other to see who could get hit on more. This couple, by the way, is no longer together.

What to Do About Dial-Toning

If you are planning to dial-tone others, consider this: 52 percent of the survey respondents indicated that they preferred direct rejection over being given contact info and then ignored later. Directly communicating your lack of interest can save everyone time, effort, and guesswork and, in the long run, be the easier route to go. And just because you’ve encountered some Cersei Lannisters or Severus Snapes who’ve taken rejection poorly in the past doesn’t mean that everyone will be like that.

If you do get dial-toned yourself, keep things in proper perspective. It may be tough to get your hopes up and then have them later deflate slowly like a twice-baked soufflé. Nevertheless, it’s always better to know sooner than later what someone is really like and what that person really thinks of you. So, at least that person didn’t give you the chance to be ghosted, right?

Ultimately, dating is about looking for the right mutual fit. And a dial-toner has told you that the two of you don’t resonate with each other—albeit indirectly and maybe a bit early.
